section: 0. Techniques that work across every topic
title: Ratio / proportionality method
body: Write the formula once, mark what is constant, and scale. If $F\propto\dfrac1{r^2}$ and $r$ triples, $F$ becomes $\dfrac19$. Saves whole calculations and removes rounding errors. Typical structures: $\propto x^2$ (energy of a spring, power $\propto I^2$, intensity $\propto A^2$), $\propto\dfrac1{x^2}$ (inverse square), $\propto\sqrt x$ ($v\propto\sqrt T$).

section: 0. Techniques that work across every topic
title: Dimensional / unit checking
body: Express every term in base units (kg, m, s, A, K, mol). Homogeneity check catches missing factors. Derive a unit by rearranging: $\mathrm{N}=\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$, $\mathrm{J}=\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}}$, $\mathrm{W}=\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-3}}$, $\mathrm{Pa}=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$, $\mathrm{V}=\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-3}\,A^{-1}}$, $\Omega=\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-3}\,A^{-2}}$, $\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{A\,s}$, $\mathrm{T}=\mathrm{kg\,s^{-2}\,A^{-1}}$, $\mathrm{Hz}=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

section: 0. Techniques that work across every topic
title: Uncertainty rules
body: **Add or subtract:** add the *absolute* uncertainties. **Multiply or divide:** add the *percentage* (fractional) uncertainties. **Power $n$:** multiply the percentage uncertainty by $|n|$. $\sqrt x$: halve it. Repeated reading: $\pm\tfrac12(\text{max}-\text{min})$. A single timing of many oscillations: divide the uncertainty by the number of oscillations.

section: 0. Techniques that work across every topic
title: Graph gradient uncertainty
body: Draw the best-fit line and the **steepest and shallowest acceptable lines** (through the error bars); uncertainty $=\tfrac12(m_{\max}-m_{\min})$. Use a large triangle, at least half the line length.

section: 0. Techniques that work across every topic
title: Making a straight line
body: $y=ax^n\Rightarrow\lg y=n\lg x+\lg a$ (gradient $n$, intercept $\lg a$). $y=ae^{kx}\Rightarrow\ln y=kx+\ln a$ (gradient $k$). Know the graph for $T^2$ vs $L$, $1/v$ vs $u$, $\sqrt{}$ forms.

section: 0. Techniques that work across every topic
title: Significant figures
body: final answer to the **fewest** sig figs of the data (usually 2 or 3); never round mid-calculation. Keep 4 s.f. in working.

section: 0. Techniques that work across every topic
title: Estimation anchors
body: person mass $\sim70\ \mathrm{kg}$, height $1.7\ \mathrm m$, walking speed $1.4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, atmospheric pressure $1.0\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}$, density of water $1000\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, AA cell $1.5\ \mathrm V$, mains $230\ \mathrm V$ (UK) / lab $\sim12\ \mathrm V$, wavelength of visible light $400$–$700\ \mathrm{nm}$, sound speed in air $340\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $c=3.0\times10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, speed of a car $30\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, mass of an apple $0.1\ \mathrm{kg}$, electron mass $9.11\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$.

section: 0. Techniques that work across every topic
title: Vectors
body: Resultant by Pythagoras if perpendicular; components $F\cos\theta$ and $F\sin\theta$ (angle **to** the axis you are resolving along). **Closed triangle of forces** for equilibrium.

section: 0. Techniques that work across every topic
title: "Explain" mark patterns
body: state the principle ($\rightarrow$ cause $\rightarrow$ effect with the physical quantity named). E.g. "resistance increases, so current falls, so $V$ across the other component increases".

title: Choose the suvat equation by the missing variable
body: see below, identical to the maths M1 table (no $s$: $v=u+at$; no $a$: $s=\tfrac12(u+v)t$; no $t$: $v^2=u^2+2as$; no $v$: $s=ut+\tfrac12at^2$).

title: Area under $v$–$t$ is displacement; gradient is acceleration
body: Area under $a$–$t$ is the change in velocity. Under a force–time graph, impulse (change in momentum).

title: Vertical throw symmetry
body: time up $=\dfrac ug$, max height $\dfrac{u^2}{2g}$, equal speeds at equal heights.

title: Projectiles
body: Horizontal: $s_x=u\cos\theta\,t$ (constant velocity). Vertical: suvat with $a=-g$. For a launch and landing at the same level: time of flight $T=\dfrac{2u\sin\theta}g$, range $R=\dfrac{u^2\sin2\theta}g$, max height $H=\dfrac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$. **Complementary angles ($\theta$ and $90^\circ-\theta$) give equal range; $45^\circ$ is the maximum.**

title: Horizontally launched from a height $h$
body: $t=\sqrt{2h/g}$; horizontal range $=u\sqrt{2h/g}$; **time of flight doesn't depend on horizontal speed**.

title: Terminal velocity
body: resultant force $0$, $a=0$; weight $=$ drag (+ upthrust). Approached by a decreasing-gradient $v$–$t$ curve.

title: Relative velocity
body: $\mathbf v_{AB}=\mathbf v_A-\mathbf v_B$; rain on a moving car; boat on a river (cross the river in the shortest time by aiming straight across; reach the point opposite by aiming upstream at $\sin\theta=\dfrac{v_{\text{river}}}{v_{\text{boat}}}$).

title: Average speed over two equal distances
body: harmonic mean $\dfrac{2v_1v_2}{v_1+v_2}$.

title: $F=\dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$
body: Area under $F$–$t$ is impulse. Force on a surface by a stream (hose, hail, sand): $F=\dfrac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}\Delta v=\rho Av\times\Delta v$ — **flow rate times velocity change**.

title: Kinetic energy and momentum
body: $E_k=\dfrac{p^2}{2m}$; so for equal momenta the lighter object has more KE; for equal KE the heavier has more momentum ($p=\sqrt{2mE_k}$).

title: Collisions
body: Momentum is always conserved (vector). Elastic: KE conserved $\Leftrightarrow$ **relative speed of approach $=$ relative speed of separation**. **Equal masses, one at rest, elastic, head-on: velocities exchange.** Perfectly inelastic: $v=\dfrac{m_1u_1+m_2u_2}{m_1+m_2}$.

title: Explosions from rest
body: total momentum $0$, so $m_1v_1=-m_2v_2$, and the lighter mass gets the larger KE (energy $\propto\dfrac1m$).

title: Newton's third law pairs
body: same type of force, same magnitude, opposite direction, **on different bodies**. Weight and normal reaction on a book are **not** a pair.

title: Connected objects / lifts
body: treat the system first, then split. Lift $R=m(g\pm a)$. **Weight of a person in a lift** = reaction.

title: Moments
body: Take moments about a point where an unknown force acts to remove it. $\sum$ clockwise $=\sum$ anticlockwise and $\sum F=0$. **Couple** $=F\times$ perpendicular separation. Uniform body: weight at the midpoint.

title: $p=h\rho g$ is the *extra* pressure
body: from a liquid column. Total pressure $=p_{\text{atm}}+h\rho g$. The pressure at a given depth is independent of container shape. **Two connected columns at equal pressure:** $h_1\rho_1=h_2\rho_2$ (U-tube with two liquids).

title: Upthrust $=\rho_{\text{fluid}}Vg$ (weight of fluid displaced)
body: Floating: upthrust $=$ weight, so **fraction submerged $=\dfrac{\rho_{\text{object}}}{\rho_{\text{fluid}}}$**. Apparent weight $=W-\text{upthrust}$.

title: Hydraulic press
body: $\dfrac{F_1}{A_1}=\dfrac{F_2}{A_2}$; distances moved are in the **inverse** ratio (energy conserved).

title: Pressure from a force over an area
body: $p=\dfrac FA$; for a person on one foot vs two, area halves so pressure doubles.

title: Density of a mixture
body: $\rho=\dfrac{m_1+m_2}{V_1+V_2}$ (not the mean of densities).

title: Work $W=Fs\cos\theta$; area under $F$–$x$
body: Zero work if the force is perpendicular to the displacement. Net work $=\Delta E_k$.

title: Energy conservation first, kinematics second
body: $mgh=\tfrac12mv^2$ gives $v=\sqrt{2gh}$ for any smooth path; **mass cancels**. With losses: $E_{\text{in}}=E_{\text{out}}+E_{\text{lost}}$.

title: Power $P=Fv$
body: At **maximum speed** driving force $=$ resistive force, so $v_{\max}=\dfrac P{F_R}$. Uphill: $P=(F_R+mg\sin\theta)v$.

title: Efficiency
body: $=\dfrac{\text{useful output}}{\text{total input}}$. For a chain of machines, multiply efficiencies.

title: Fluid flow: wind and water
body: Mass flow rate $\dfrac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}=\rho Av$, so power in the flow $P=\tfrac12\rho Av^3$ (**$P\propto v^3$**, $\propto r^2$). Hydro: $P=\rho gh\times\dfrac{\Delta V}{\Delta t}$ (volume rate). Doubling wind speed gives eight times the power.

title: Falling in an energy-conserving loop
body: use $mgh$ differences, not kinematics; the loop-the-loop minimum release height is $2.5R$ (just completing a vertical circle).

title: Gravitational PE change
body: $\Delta E_p=mg\Delta h$, only the vertical height matters.

title: Kinetic energy ratio
body: $E_k\propto v^2$; speed doubles, KE quadruples, braking distance quadruples ($d=\dfrac{v^2}{2a}$).

title: Energy per unit of time units
body: $1\ \mathrm{kWh}=3.6\times10^6\ \mathrm J$.

title: Hooke's law, $F=kx$; energy $E=\tfrac12Fx=\tfrac12kx^2$
body: **Doubling the extension quadruples the energy.** Energy $=$ area under the $F$–$x$ graph (also for non-linear curves, count squares).

title: Springs combined
body: **Series:** $\dfrac1k=\dfrac1{k_1}+\dfrac1{k_2}$ (each carries the full load; extensions add). **Parallel:** $k=k_1+k_2$ (load shared, extension equal). Same logic as capacitors, opposite to resistors.

title: Stress, strain, Young modulus
body: $\sigma=\dfrac FA$, $\varepsilon=\dfrac xL$, $E=\dfrac\sigma\varepsilon=\dfrac{FL}{Ax}$. The gradient of stress–strain is $E$; **$k=\dfrac{EA}L$**. Strain energy per unit volume $=\tfrac12\sigma\varepsilon$ ($=\dfrac{\sigma^2}{2E}$).

title: Wire diameter: area $\propto d^2$
body: Halving diameter quarters area; doubling the length doubles extension for the same force. Uncertainty in $A$ is **twice** the percentage uncertainty in $d$.

title: Force–extension vs stress–strain
body: the first depends on the specimen; the second is a material property.

title: Limit of proportionality / elastic limit / yield
body: beyond the elastic limit the wire does not return to its original length (permanent extension). Ductile, brittle, polymeric (rubber hysteresis; the area between the loading and unloading curves is the energy dissipated as thermal energy).

title: Energy conversion in a spring launcher
body: $\tfrac12kx^2=\tfrac12mv^2+mgh$ in one line.

title: Wave equation
body: $v=f\lambda$; $T=\dfrac1f$. When the medium changes, $f$ stays constant and $\lambda\propto v$.

title: Intensity
body: $I=\dfrac PA$; $I\propto A_{\text{amp}}^2$ (amplitude squared); for a point source $I\propto\dfrac1{r^2}$. Doubling the distance quarters the intensity; doubling the amplitude gives four times the intensity.

title: Phase difference
body: $\Delta\phi=\dfrac{2\pi\Delta x}\lambda=360^\circ\dfrac{\Delta x}\lambda$ (path difference), or $360^\circ\dfrac{\Delta t}T$ (time difference). From a displacement–position graph, count the fraction of a wavelength between the two points.

title: Doppler (source moving)
body: $f_o=\dfrac{f_sv}{v\pm v_s}$ ($-$ approaching, $+$ receding). **Higher pitch approaching**.

title: Malus's law
body: $I=I_0\cos^2\theta$ through a second polariser at angle $\theta$; unpolarised light halves on the first polariser. Crossed polarisers block all light.

title: Wave speed from a graph
body: speed $=\dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}$ or $f\lambda$; a **displacement–position** graph gives $\lambda$; **displacement–time** gives $T$.

title: EM spectrum order (long to short $\lambda$)
body: radio, microwaves, infrared, visible (red to violet), ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma. All travel at $c$ in vacuum. **Mnemonic:** *R*abbits *M*ate *I*n *V*arious *U*nusual *X*-rated *G*ardens.

title: Double slit
body: $\lambda=\dfrac{ax}D$ ($a$ slit separation, $x$ fringe spacing, $D$ screen distance). **Measure across many fringes** to cut the uncertainty. Wider spacing $x$ for longer $\lambda$ or larger $D$, smaller $a$.

title: Diffraction grating
body: $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$ with $d=\dfrac1{\text{lines per metre}}$. **Maximum order** $n_{\max}=\left\lfloor\dfrac d\lambda\right\rfloor$ (as $\sin\theta\le1$). **Total number of maxima** $=2n_{\max}+1$. Same $\lambda$, more lines per mm give larger angles and fewer orders.

title: Path difference conditions
body: constructive: $n\lambda$ (in phase sources); destructive: $(n+\tfrac12)\lambda$. For sources in antiphase, swap them.

title: Stationary waves on a string (fixed both ends)
body: $f_n=\dfrac{nv}{2L}$, **harmonics $1,2,3,\dots$**; $v=\sqrt{T/\mu}$ (not on data booklet) so $f\propto\sqrt T$. Node-to-node spacing $=\dfrac\lambda2$.

title: Closed pipe (one end closed)
body: **odd harmonics only**, $f=\dfrac{(2n-1)v}{4L}$; fundamental $\dfrac v{4L}$; node at closed end, antinode at open. **Open pipe:** all harmonics, $f=\dfrac{nv}{2L}$. A closed pipe's fundamental is **half** that of an open one of the same length.

title: Find $v$ from resonance in a tube
body: the difference in two consecutive resonance lengths $=\dfrac\lambda2$, so $v=2f(L_2-L_1)$ and the **end correction cancels**.

title: Stationary vs progressive
body: stationary waves have nodes, constant phase within a loop (adjacent loops $180^\circ$ out of phase), amplitude varying with position and no energy transfer.

title: Rayleigh criterion (A Level)
body: $\theta\approx\dfrac\lambda b$ for a slit of width $b$ (for a circular aperture $1.22\lambda/b$).

title: Single-slit diffraction
body: first minimum at $b\sin\theta=\lambda$; central maximum is twice as wide as the others.

title: Charge and current
body: $Q=It$; $V=\dfrac WQ$ (energy per unit charge); $E=VIt$. $1\ \mathrm{kWh}=3.6\ \mathrm{MJ}$.

title: Drift velocity
body: $I=nAvq$. **Same current, thinner wire gives higher drift speed** ($v\propto\dfrac1A$); a semiconductor has far fewer carriers (small $n$) so a much larger $v$.

title: Resistance
body: $R=\dfrac{\rho L}A$; **doubling the length doubles $R$; doubling the diameter divides $R$ by $4$**; stretching a wire at constant volume (new length $kL$) multiplies $R$ by $k^2$.

title: Power: the three forms
body: $P=VI=I^2R=\dfrac{V^2}R$. **Same current: $P\propto R$ (series). Same voltage: $P\propto\dfrac1R$ (parallel/mains).** Doubling the current quadruples the heat.

title: Parallel resistors
body: two: $R=\dfrac{R_1R_2}{R_1+R_2}$ (product over sum); $n$ equal: $\dfrac Rn$. **A parallel combination is always smaller than the smallest branch.** Parallel of unknown value $R_x$ giving $R_T$: $R_x=\dfrac{R_TR_1}{R_1-R_T}$.

title: Potential divider
body: $V_{\text{out}}=V_{\text{in}}\dfrac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}$. **Voltage splits in proportion to resistance.** With a thermistor/LDR: resistance falls when hot/bright, so the share across it falls.

title: Loaded potential divider
body: a load in parallel with $R_2$ lowers $R_2$'s effective value and so $V_{\text{out}}$ falls. A **sliding contact** varies $V_{\text{out}}$ from $0$ to $V_{\text{in}}$.

title: EMF and internal resistance
body: $E=I(R+r)=V+Ir$. Plot $V$ against $I$: **gradient $=-r$, intercept $=E$** (at $I=0$). **Terminal voltage falls when current rises.** Short-circuit current $=\dfrac Er$.

title: Maximum power transfer (A Level favourite)
body: load power is greatest when $R=r$, with $P_{\max}=\dfrac{E^2}{4r}$ and efficiency $50\%$.

title: Kirchhoff
body: **first law** (current in $=$ current out at a junction, conservation of charge); **second law** ($\sum E=\sum IR$ around a loop; conservation of energy). Write a loop equation for each independent loop.

title: Series cells
body: emf adds, internal resistances add. **Identical cells in parallel:** emf stays $E$, internal resistance $\dfrac rn$.

title: Ammeter and voltmeter
body: ammeter in series (low resistance); voltmeter in parallel (high resistance). Resistance of a lamp changes with temperature, so it does not obey Ohm's law (curved $I$–$V$).

title: I–V graphs
body: resistance at a point is $V/I$ (**not** the gradient unless the graph is a straight line through the origin).

title: Potentiometer (A Level)
body: balance length gives $\dfrac{E_1}{E_2}=\dfrac{l_1}{l_2}$ at no current (so it measures a true emf).

title: Kilowatt-hour cost
body: energy $=P(\mathrm{kW})\times t(\mathrm h)$; cost $=$ energy $\times$ rate.

title: Fuse choice
body: $I=\dfrac PV$; choose the next rating above it.

title: Quarks
body: up $+\tfrac23e$, down $-\tfrac13e$, strange $-\tfrac13e$. **Proton uud** ($+1$), **neutron udd** ($0$). Antiquarks have the opposite charge. **Baryon** $=qqq$ (baryon number $+1$), **meson** $=q\bar q$ (baryon number $0$).

title: Beta decays
body: $\beta^-$: $n\to p+e^-+\bar\nu_e$ (**d turns into u**); $\beta^+$: $p\to n+e^++\nu_e$ (**u turns into d**). **Always check conservation of charge, baryon number and lepton number** (electron $+1$, positron $-1$, neutrino $+1$, antineutrino $-1$).

title: Conservation checklist
body: charge, baryon number, lepton number; **momentum and energy**. Strangeness is conserved only in the strong interaction (beyond spec).

title: Nuclide balancing
body: top (nucleon) numbers sum equal; bottom (proton) numbers sum equal. $\alpha$: $-4$ in $A$, $-2$ in $Z$. $\beta^-$: $Z\to Z+1$. $\beta^+$: $Z\to Z-1$. $\gamma$: no change.

title: Energy conversions
body: $1\ \mathrm{eV}=1.60\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm J$; $1\ \mathrm u=1.66\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}\equiv931.5\ \mathrm{MeV}/c^2$. $E=mc^2$: mass in u $\times931.5$ gives MeV directly.

title: Leptons and hadrons
body: leptons (electron, neutrino) are fundamental and don't feel the strong force; hadrons are made of quarks.

title: Fundamental forces' ranges (A Level reading)
body: strong (short, $\sim10^{-15}$ m), weak (very short), EM and gravity (infinite).

section: 7. A Level: circular motion and gravitation (12–13)
title: Circular motion equations
body: $v=r\omega$, $\omega=\dfrac{2\pi}T=2\pi f$, $a=\dfrac{v^2}r=\omega^2r$, $F=\dfrac{mv^2}r=m\omega^2r$. **The centripetal force is the resultant of real forces towards the centre, never an extra force.**

section: 7. A Level: circular motion and gravitation (12–13)
title: Conical pendulum / banked track / car on a bend
body: $\tan\theta=\dfrac{v^2}{rg}$ (banked, no friction). Maximum speed on a flat bend: $v=\sqrt{\mu gr}$.

section: 7. A Level: circular motion and gravitation (12–13)
title: Vertical circle
body: at the **top** need $T+mg=\dfrac{mv^2}r$ so the minimum speed is $v=\sqrt{gr}$ (string just taut); at the **bottom** minimum speed to complete the circle is $\sqrt{5gr}$ (by energy conservation); tension at the bottom exceeds at the top by $6mg$.

section: 7. A Level: circular motion and gravitation (12–13)
title: Gravitational force and field
body: $F=\dfrac{GMm}{r^2}$, $g=\dfrac{GM}{r^2}$ (inverse square). **At altitude $h$:** $g'=g\left(\dfrac R{R+h}\right)^2$. Surface: $g=\tfrac43\pi G\rho R$ (uniform sphere).

section: 7. A Level: circular motion and gravitation (12–13)
title: Orbits: the key identity
body: gravity $=$ centripetal, so $v=\sqrt{\dfrac{GM}r}$ and $T^2=\dfrac{4\pi^2}{GM}r^3$ (**Kepler: $T^2\propto r^3$**). **Mass of the orbiting body cancels.** Use the ratio method: $\dfrac{T_1^2}{T_2^2}=\dfrac{r_1^3}{r_2^3}$ (Moon $27.3$ d at $3.84\times10^8$ m).

section: 7. A Level: circular motion and gravitation (12–13)
title: Geostationary
body: $T=24\ \mathrm h$, equatorial, same direction as Earth's rotation, $r\approx4.22\times10^7\ \mathrm m$ (height $\approx3.6\times10^7\ \mathrm m$).

section: 7. A Level: circular motion and gravitation (12–13)
title: Potential and orbital energy
body: $\phi=-\dfrac{GM}r$; potential energy $-\dfrac{GMm}r$. In a circular orbit: **$E_k=\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$, $E_p=-\dfrac{GMm}r$, $E_{\text{total}}=-\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$**. So $E_p=-2E_k$ and $E_{\text{total}}=-E_k$. A lower orbit has **more** KE, lower (more negative) total energy.

section: 7. A Level: circular motion and gravitation (12–13)
title: Escape speed
body: $v_{\text{esc}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}R}=\sqrt{2gR}$, which is $\sqrt2\times$ the circular-orbit speed at the surface. Earth: $11.2\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$.

section: 7. A Level: circular motion and gravitation (12–13)
title: Work done in moving between two points
body: $W=m\Delta\phi$. Area under a $g$–$r$ graph is $-\Delta\phi$.

section: 7. A Level: circular motion and gravitation (12–13)
title: Gravitational vs electric analogy
body: $\dfrac{GMm}{r^2}\leftrightarrow\dfrac{Qq}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2}$; gravity is always attractive.

section: 7. A Level: circular motion and gravitation (12–13)
title: Field between two bodies
body: $g=0$ at the neutral point where $\dfrac{M_1}{r_1^2}=\dfrac{M_2}{r_2^2}$, i.e. $\dfrac{r_1}{r_2}=\sqrt{\dfrac{M_1}{M_2}}$.

section: 8. A Level: gases and thermal physics (14–15)
title: Ideal gas
body: $pV=nRT=NkT$ with $R=8.31$, $k=1.38\times10^{-23}$. **Ratio form** for a fixed quantity: $\dfrac{p_1V_1}{T_1}=\dfrac{p_2V_2}{T_2}$ (**always in kelvin**). Density: $\rho=\dfrac{pM}{RT}$.

section: 8. A Level: gases and thermal physics (14–15)
title: Kinetic theory
body: $pV=\tfrac13Nm\langle c^2\rangle$, $p=\tfrac13\rho\langle c^2\rangle$. **Average KE per molecule** $=\tfrac32kT$ (**depends only on $T$**); $c_{\text{rms}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{3kT}m}=\sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}M}$. Lighter gas molecules move faster at the same $T$ ($v\propto\dfrac1{\sqrt m}$).

section: 8. A Level: gases and thermal physics (14–15)
title: Number of molecules
body: $N=\dfrac{pV}{kT}=nN_A$. Internal energy of an ideal monatomic gas $U=\tfrac32NkT=\tfrac32nRT$.

section: 8. A Level: gases and thermal physics (14–15)
title: First law
body: $\Delta U=q+w$ (**$w$ is work done *on* the gas**). Work done by an expanding gas $=p\Delta V$ (area under $pV$). Isothermal: $\Delta U=0$ so $q=-w$. Constant volume: $w=0$. Adiabatic: $q=0$.

section: 8. A Level: gases and thermal physics (14–15)
title: Temperature scales
body: $T/\mathrm K=\theta/^\circ\mathrm C+273.15$. A change of $1\ \mathrm K$ equals $1^\circ\mathrm C$.

section: 8. A Level: gases and thermal physics (14–15)
title: Heating
body: $Q=mc\Delta T$, $Q=mL$; **electrical heater: $Pt=mc\Delta T$**. For specific latent heat with losses, take the **difference of two runs** to cancel the constant loss.

section: 8. A Level: gases and thermal physics (14–15)
title: Mixing/thermal equilibrium
body: heat lost $=$ heat gained. Mixing two amounts of water: $T_f=\dfrac{m_1T_1+m_2T_2}{m_1+m_2}$ (same $c$).

section: 8. A Level: gases and thermal physics (14–15)
title: Specific heat vs latent heat graph
body: flat sections are phase changes; **steeper line means smaller $c$** (for constant power).

section: 8. A Level: gases and thermal physics (14–15)
title: Moles and atoms
body: $N=nN_A$, mass $=nM$, $1\ \mathrm{mol}=6.02\times10^{23}$.

section: 8. A Level: gases and thermal physics (14–15)
title: Brownian motion (qualitative)
body: random molecular collisions on smoke particles.

title: SHM defining equation
body: $a=-\omega^2x$. $\omega=2\pi f=\dfrac{2\pi}T$. **Period independent of amplitude.**

title: Displacement, velocity, acceleration
body: from the **equilibrium** start $x=x_0\sin\omega t$, $v=v_0\cos\omega t$, $v_0=\omega x_0$, $a_{\max}=\omega^2x_0$. **From an extreme position** $x=x_0\cos\omega t$. **Velocity at any displacement:** $v=\pm\omega\sqrt{x_0^2-x^2}$ — no time needed.

title: Energy in SHM
body: total $E=\tfrac12m\omega^2x_0^2$; $E_k=\tfrac12m\omega^2(x_0^2-x^2)$; $E_p=\tfrac12m\omega^2x^2$. **$E_k=E_p$ at $x=\dfrac{x_0}{\sqrt2}$.** Total energy $\propto x_0^2$ and $\propto f^2$.

title: Periods
body: simple pendulum $T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac Lg}$ (small angles); mass–spring $T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac mk}$. **Ratio method:** quadrupling $m$ doubles $T$. Spring in series/parallel: use effective $k$.

title: Graph shapes
body: $a$ against $x$ is a straight line of gradient $-\omega^2$ through the origin (use to find $T$). $v$ against $x$ is an ellipse. $E_k$ and $E_p$ against $x$ are parabolas (opposite). Against $t$, $E_k$ and $E_p$ oscillate at **twice** the SHM frequency.

title: Damping and resonance
body: light damping $\rightarrow$ amplitude falls slowly; **critical damping** gives the fastest return without oscillating; heavy damping slows the return. At resonance (driving $f=$ natural $f_0$) the amplitude peaks; **more damping lowers and broadens the peak** and moves it to slightly lower frequency.

title: Phase
body: $v$ leads $x$ by $\dfrac\pi2$; $a$ is in antiphase with $x$.

title: Finding $\omega$ from two data points
body: $v^2=\omega^2(x_0^2-x^2)$ for two pairs $\rightarrow$ solve for $\omega^2$ and $x_0^2$ (subtract).

section: 10. A Level: electric fields and capacitance (17–18)
title: Coulomb and field
body: $F=\dfrac{Qq}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2}$, $E=\dfrac Q{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2}$ (point charge), $E=\dfrac Vd$ (uniform field between plates), $F=qE$. **Same inverse-square ratio method as gravity.**

section: 10. A Level: electric fields and capacitance (17–18)
title: Electric potential
body: $V=\dfrac Q{4\pi\varepsilon_0r}$ (scalar; sign matters); work $=q\Delta V$; $E=-\dfrac{dV}{dx}$ (gradient of the $V$–$r$ graph, sign), and area under $E$–$r$ gives $-\Delta V$. $E_k$ gained by a charge through $V$: $\tfrac12mv^2=qV$.

section: 10. A Level: electric fields and capacitance (17–18)
title: Charged particle in a uniform field
body: parabolic path like a projectile with "$g$" replaced by $\dfrac{qE}m$; electrons: $a=\dfrac{eV}{md}$.

section: 10. A Level: electric fields and capacitance (17–18)
title: Capacitors
body: $C=\dfrac QV$; **energy** $W=\tfrac12QV=\tfrac12CV^2=\dfrac{Q^2}{2C}$ (area under $V$–$Q$). **Parallel plates:** $C=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}d$ (so $C\propto A$, $C\propto\dfrac1d$).

section: 10. A Level: electric fields and capacitance (17–18)
title: Combining capacitors
body: **parallel add** $C=C_1+C_2$; **series** $\dfrac1C=\dfrac1{C_1}+\dfrac1{C_2}$ — the **opposite of resistors** (series capacitors share the same charge; voltages divide inversely to $C$).

section: 10. A Level: electric fields and capacitance (17–18)
title: RC discharge
body: $Q=Q_0e^{-t/RC}$, same form for $I$ and $V$; **time constant $\tau=RC$**; after one $\tau$ the quantity falls to $37\%$ ($e^{-1}$); **half-life $t_{1/2}=RC\ln2\approx0.693\,RC$**. **Charging:** $V=V_0(1-e^{-t/RC})$ reaches $63\%$ after $\tau$. Gradient of $Q$–$t$ at $t=0$: $I_0=\dfrac{V_0}R$.

section: 10. A Level: electric fields and capacitance (17–18)
title: Using logs
body: $\ln V=\ln V_0-\dfrac t{RC}$; the gradient of $\ln V$ against $t$ is $-\dfrac1{RC}$.

section: 10. A Level: electric fields and capacitance (17–18)
title: Energy lost in charging through a resistor
body: half of the supply's work $QV$ goes into the capacitor, half is dissipated as heat.

section: 10. A Level: electric fields and capacitance (17–18)
title: Capacitor smoothing
body: a larger $C$ or $R$ means a slower discharge (smoother output of a rectifier).

title: Force on a conductor / charge
body: $F=BIL\sin\theta$, $F=Bqv\sin\theta$. **Fleming's left-hand rule** for the direction of the force. **Circular motion in a magnetic field:** $Bqv=\dfrac{mv^2}r\Rightarrow r=\dfrac{mv}{Bq}=\dfrac p{Bq}$, and period $T=\dfrac{2\pi m}{Bq}$ **independent of $v$**.

title: Velocity selector
body: undeflected when $qE=Bqv$, i.e. $v=\dfrac EB$.

title: Hall effect
body: $V_H=\dfrac{BI}{ntq}$ ($t$ thickness); used to find $n$ or $B$ (a Hall probe). A thinner semiconductor strip with small $n$ gives a bigger voltage.

title: Field formulae
body: long straight wire $B=\dfrac{\mu_0I}{2\pi r}$; flat coil/solenoid $B=\mu_0nI$ ($n$ turns per metre; $B$ doubles if $I$ doubles). Force between parallel wires $\dfrac FL=\dfrac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{2\pi d}$ (attract if currents in the same direction).

title: Flux and Faraday
body: $\Phi=BA\cos\theta$, flux linkage $N\Phi$, $|\mathcal E|=N\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt}$. **Lenz:** the induced current opposes the change. EMF of a straight rod moving across a field: $\mathcal E=Blv$ (**sweeps area at rate $Blv$**). EMF of a rotating coil: $\mathcal E=BAN\omega\sin\omega t$, peak $BAN\omega$.

title: Induced EMF from a graph
body: **gradient of the flux–time graph** (not the height).

title: Transformer
body: $\dfrac{V_s}{V_p}=\dfrac{N_s}{N_p}$; for an ideal one $V_pI_p=V_sI_s$ (so step-up voltage means step-down current). Transmission losses $P=I^2R$ — **step the voltage up to cut $I$**. Real transformer losses: resistance of windings, eddy currents (laminated core), hysteresis, flux leakage.

title: AC
body: $V_{\text{rms}}=\dfrac{V_0}{\sqrt2}$, $I_{\text{rms}}=\dfrac{I_0}{\sqrt2}$, mean power $=\tfrac12I_0V_0=\dfrac{V_0^2}{2R}$ (half the peak power). **Reading a CRO:** $V_{\text{peak}}=$ divisions $\times$ volts per div; period $=$ divisions $\times$ time-base; $f=\dfrac1T$.

title: Rectification
body: a diode gives half-wave; a bridge gives full-wave; a smoothing capacitor reduces the ripple.

title: Lenz-law direction trick
body: the induced current always creates a field that **opposes the flux change**: moving a magnet towards a coil, the near face is the same pole as the magnet.

section: 12. A Level: quantum, nuclear, medical, astronomy (22–25)
title: Photon energy
body: $E=hf=\dfrac{hc}\lambda$. **Quick conversion** (not on data booklet): $\lambda(\mathrm{nm})\times E(\mathrm{eV})\approx1240$. A $2.0\ \mathrm{eV}$ photon is $620\ \mathrm{nm}$.

section: 12. A Level: quantum, nuclear, medical, astronomy (22–25)
title: Photoelectric effect
body: $hf=\Phi+E_{k,\max}$ where $\Phi=hf_0$. $eV_s=E_{k,\max}$ (stopping potential). **Intensity** changes the **number** of photoelectrons (current), **not** their max energy. $E_k$ against $f$: gradient $h$, $x$-intercept $f_0$, $y$-intercept $-\Phi$.

section: 12. A Level: quantum, nuclear, medical, astronomy (22–25)
title: de Broglie
body: $\lambda=\dfrac hp=\dfrac h{mv}$. For an electron accelerated through $V$: $\lambda=\dfrac h{\sqrt{2meV}}\approx\dfrac{1.23}{\sqrt{V}}\ \mathrm{nm}$ (V in volts). Doubling the accelerating voltage divides $\lambda$ by $\sqrt2$.

section: 12. A Level: quantum, nuclear, medical, astronomy (22–25)
title: Energy levels
body: $hf=E_2-E_1$ for emission/absorption; **number of possible spectral lines** from level $n$: $\dfrac{n(n-1)}2$. Line spectra evidence for discrete levels; continuous spectrum from hot solids.

section: 12. A Level: quantum, nuclear, medical, astronomy (22–25)
title: X-rays
body: minimum wavelength $\lambda_{\min}=\dfrac{hc}{eV}$.

section: 12. A Level: quantum, nuclear, medical, astronomy (22–25)
title: Wave–particle evidence
body: electron diffraction (wave), photoelectric effect (particle).

section: 12. A Level: quantum, nuclear, medical, astronomy (22–25)
title: Decay
body: $N=N_0e^{-\lambda t}$ (also $A$, count rate), $A=\lambda N$, $\lambda=\dfrac{\ln2}{t_{1/2}}$. **After $n$ half-lives the fraction is $\left(\tfrac12\right)^n$**; use it before exponentials. Remaining fraction after time $t$: $2^{-t/t_{1/2}}$.

section: 12. A Level: quantum, nuclear, medical, astronomy (22–25)
title: Activity ratios
body: activity of a source $\propto N$; for two sources, the one with the shorter half-life has the higher activity for the same number of nuclei.

section: 12. A Level: quantum, nuclear, medical, astronomy (22–25)
title: Background correction
body: corrected rate $=$ measured $-$ background. **Measure the background first, over a long time**.

section: 12. A Level: quantum, nuclear, medical, astronomy (22–25)
title: Binding energy and mass defect
body: $\Delta m=Zm_p+(A-Z)m_n-m_{\text{nucleus}}$; $E_B=\Delta mc^2$, with $\Delta m$ in u $\times931.5=$ MeV. **Binding energy per nucleon** peaks at iron (Fe-56): fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy ones both release energy.

section: 12. A Level: quantum, nuclear, medical, astronomy (22–25)
title: Energy released in a reaction
body: $Q=\left(\sum m_{\text{reactants}}-\sum m_{\text{products}}\right)c^2$; use atomic or nuclear masses consistently. In MeV: $\Delta m(\mathrm u)\times931.5$.

section: 12. A Level: quantum, nuclear, medical, astronomy (22–25)
title: Rutherford and the nucleus
body: most $\alpha$ pass undeflected (atom mostly empty), a few deflect through large angles (small dense positive nucleus); radius $R=r_0A^{1/3}$ so **density is the same for all nuclei** ($\sim10^{17}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$).

section: 12. A Level: quantum, nuclear, medical, astronomy (22–25)
title: Nuclear radius
body: $R=r_0A^{1/3}$ with $r_0\approx1.2\ \mathrm{fm}$.

section: 12. A Level: quantum, nuclear, medical, astronomy (22–25)
title: Safety
body: inverse-square law for distance; shielding; $\alpha$ stopped by paper, $\beta$ by aluminium, $\gamma$ by thick lead (intensity falls exponentially).

section: 12. A Level: quantum, nuclear, medical, astronomy (22–25)
title: Attenuation
body: $I=I_0e^{-\mu x}$; **half-value thickness** $x_{1/2}=\dfrac{\ln2}\mu$. Same structure as radioactive decay.

section: 12. A Level: quantum, nuclear, medical, astronomy (22–25)
title: Acoustic impedance
body: $Z=\rho c$; **intensity reflection coefficient** $\alpha=\dfrac{(Z_2-Z_1)^2}{(Z_2+Z_1)^2}$; **gel** removes the air gap (large mismatch) so more is transmitted.

section: 12. A Level: quantum, nuclear, medical, astronomy (22–25)
title: Ultrasound imaging
body: depth $=\dfrac{vt}{2}$ (echo travels there and back).

section: 12. A Level: quantum, nuclear, medical, astronomy (22–25)
title: X-ray CT, MRI, PET
body: CT combines many projections; MRI uses RF resonance of protons in a field gradient; PET uses positron annihilation to give two $0.511\ \mathrm{MeV}$ photons in opposite directions.

section: 12. A Level: quantum, nuclear, medical, astronomy (22–25)
title: Luminosity–flux
body: $F=\dfrac L{4\pi d^2}$ (inverse square). Standard candles $\rightarrow$ distance by comparing $F$.

section: 12. A Level: quantum, nuclear, medical, astronomy (22–25)
title: Stefan–Boltzmann
body: $L=4\pi r^2\sigma T^4$. **Ratio method:** doubling radius $\times4$ in $L$; doubling $T$ $\times16$. For two stars $\dfrac{L_1}{L_2}=\left(\dfrac{r_1}{r_2}\right)^2\left(\dfrac{T_1}{T_2}\right)^4$.

section: 12. A Level: quantum, nuclear, medical, astronomy (22–25)
title: Wien
body: $\lambda_{\max}T=2.898\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m\,K}$ — hotter means bluer. Estimate a star's temperature from its peak wavelength.

section: 12. A Level: quantum, nuclear, medical, astronomy (22–25)
title: Redshift and Hubble
body: $\dfrac{\Delta\lambda}\lambda\approx\dfrac vc$ (for $v\ll c$); $v=H_0d$; **age of the universe $\sim\dfrac1{H_0}$**. Convert units: $1\ \mathrm{pc}=3.09\times10^{16}\ \mathrm m$, $1\ \mathrm{ly}=9.46\times10^{15}\ \mathrm m$, $1\ \mathrm{AU}=1.50\times10^{11}\ \mathrm m$.

section: 12. A Level: quantum, nuclear, medical, astronomy (22–25)
title: Parallax
body: $d(\mathrm{pc})=\dfrac1{p(\mathrm{arcsec})}$.

section: 12. A Level: quantum, nuclear, medical, astronomy (22–25)
title: Evolution of stars
body: low mass: main sequence $\rightarrow$ red giant $\rightarrow$ planetary nebula $\rightarrow$ white dwarf; high mass: red supergiant $\rightarrow$ supernova $\rightarrow$ neutron star / black hole.

section: 12. A Level: quantum, nuclear, medical, astronomy (22–25)
title: Cosmic microwave background
body: $\sim2.7\ \mathrm K$, redshifted relic of the hot early universe; evidence for the Big Bang along with Hubble's law and the abundance of light elements.

section: 0. Techniques that work across every topic
title: Build the results table from the intended graph
body: In a practical question, decide the $x$- and $y$-axis quantities before taking readings, then put both raw measurements and every transformed quantity needed for the graph in one table. This prevents a last-minute recalculation and makes the unit in each heading explicit, for example $I/\mathrm{mA}$ rather than just $\mathrm{mA}$.

section: 0. Techniques that work across every topic
title: A false origin does not give an intercept
body: If the graph axis starts above zero, take a convenient point on the fitted line and calculate $c=y-mx$; the point where the line meets the drawn axis is not $c$. Substitute the result back into $y=mx+c$ at another point to catch a scale or sign slip.

section: 0. Techniques that work across every topic
title: Compare a result with its allowed uncertainty
source: Cambridge 9702 syllabus 2025–27 p47; 9702 s24 ms 34 p7
body: When two experimental values of a proposed constant are compared, calculate their percentage difference using the denominator requested in the question, then compare it with the stated percentage uncertainty. Finish with an explicit conclusion about whether the data support the relationship; a bare claim that the values are "close" cannot establish agreement.

section: 0. Techniques that work across every topic
title: Keep graph powers of ten in the gradient
body: For an axis labelled $y/(10^{-3}\,\mathrm m)$, a rise of $4.0$ on the paper represents $4.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm m$ in the physical gradient. Write the two coordinate differences with their axis factors before dividing, then check the resulting gradient unit as $[y]/[x]$.

section: 0. Techniques that work across every topic
title: Subtraction follows decimal places
body: For a measured extension $L-L_0$ or temperature rise $T_2-T_1$, retain decimal places justified by the two readings; the result can have fewer significant figures than either original measurement. Use that difference, rather than the raw lengths or temperatures, when justifying precision in a quantity calculated from it.

section: 0. Techniques that work across every topic
title: Make uncertainty match the measurement
body: When an edge or event is hard to judge, estimate uncertainty from that judgement as well as instrument resolution; a protractor's smallest division need not be the uncertainty of a fuzzy angle. Check that an uncertainty in time or length is plausible relative to the observed scatter and the measurement method.

section: 0. Techniques that work across every topic
title: Recover intercept uncertainty from two lines
source: Cambridge 9702 syllabus 2025–27 p52; examiner report 9702 June 2024 p60
body: On a Paper 5 graph, calculate $c_{\rm best}=y-m_{\rm best}x$ and $c_{\rm worst}=y-m_{\rm worst}x$ using points on the respective drawn lines. Then use $|c_{\rm best}-c_{\rm worst}|$ as the absolute intercept uncertainty; gradient percentage uncertainty alone does not give intercept uncertainty.

section: 0. Techniques that work across every topic
title: Take logarithms of numbers with declared units
source: Cambridge 9702 syllabus 2025–27 p52; examiner report 9702 June 2024 p64
body: In a table or graph write $\lg(L/\mathrm{cm})$ or $\ln(t/\mathrm s)$, so the logarithm's argument is dimensionless; the plotted logarithm itself has no unit. Use $10^c$ to undo an $\lg$ intercept and $e^c$ to undo an $\ln$ intercept, checking the chosen base before calculating a constant.

section: 0. Techniques that work across every topic
title: Transform log-intercept uncertainty before quoting a constant
body: If a graph gives $c=\lg k$, calculate $k=10^c$ and compare it with $10^{c\pm\Delta c}$; for $c=\ln k$, use $e^{c\pm\Delta c}$. The percentage uncertainty in $k$ is not the percentage uncertainty in $c$, and the upper and lower changes need not be equal.

section: 0. Techniques that work across every topic
title: Fit the line, not the end readings
source: Cambridge 9702 syllabus 2025–27 p46; examiner report 9702 June 2024 p60
body: For a graph with scatter, draw the trend with points balanced on both sides and mark an anomalous point if it must be ignored. Read two easy grid intersections on the line, separated by more than half its length, for the gradient; they do not need to be measured data points.

section: 0. Techniques that work across every topic
title: State how the graph tests the model
body: After naming axes, state the predicted line shape and intercept: for $y=kx$, the relationship is supported by a straight line through the origin, while $y=kx+c$ permits a nonzero intercept. State how the requested constant comes from the gradient or intercept; writing only $y=mx+c$ leaves the physical test unstated.

section: 0. Techniques that work across every topic
title: Turn a limitation into a paired improvement
source: Cambridge 9702 syllabus 2025–27 p47; 9702 s24 ms 34 p8
body: Name the measured quantity and why it is uncertain, then propose a change that removes that cause: an uncertain release position can use a fixed stop, and a hard-to-see instant can use video frames or a sensor. Check that the proposed apparatus measures the required quantity directly or gives a stated route to calculate it.

section: 0. Techniques that work across every topic
title: Two values test agreement, not a trend
body: If a practical question asks whether a formula holds, two values of its constant may be compared with a stated tolerance, but they cannot establish the shape of the whole relationship. Suggest several distinct independent-variable settings and a graph when evaluating the range of validity.

section: 0. Techniques that work across every topic
title: State what a light gate actually times
body: In a Paper 5 velocity plan, give the interrupting flag's length $l$ and its blocking time $\Delta t$, then calculate $v\approx l/\Delta t$ for a sufficiently short flag. Check that $l$ is short enough that speed does not change appreciably while it passes the gate.

title: Set a signed-motion ledger
body: Before using suvat or momentum, choose a positive direction and write each velocity and acceleration with a sign; a thrown object's velocity changes sign at the top even though its speed is positive. Substitute the signed values into one equation and check that the answer's direction agrees with the sketch.

title: Split motion at a turning point
body: If an object reverses direction, solve for the turning time using $v=0$ and treat the two legs separately when asked for total distance. Displacement can be calculated in one signed step, whereas distance is the sum of the magnitudes of the legs.

title: Use the absolute graph areas for distance
body: On a velocity–time graph that crosses the time axis, add areas with signs for displacement but add their absolute values for distance travelled. Distance must be at least the magnitude of displacement, giving an immediate check.

title: Use input power to bypass changing acceleration
body: When a motor delivers constant useful power $P$ for time $t$, its energy output is $Pt$ even while the driving force $P/v$ and acceleration change. Equate $Pt$ to the stated gains in kinetic and potential energy plus losses, checking that all terms are energies in joules.

title: Correct diameter before squaring it
body: If a micrometer has zero reading $z$, use corrected diameter $d=d_{\rm read}-z$ before calculating a wire's area $A=\pi d^2/4$; correcting the area afterward is invalid. Check several positions and perpendicular orientations if the wire may not be uniform or round, because the squared diameter magnifies any error.

title: Check refraction with an invariant ratio
body: Across a boundary, $f$ is unchanged, so $v_1/v_2=\lambda_1/\lambda_2=\sin\theta_1/\sin\theta_2$ for angles measured from the normal. If the ray bends towards the normal, both speed and wavelength must fall; this catches an inverted refractive-index ratio.

title: Gate total internal reflection by both conditions
body: A critical angle exists only for incidence from higher to lower refractive index, with $\sin c=n_2/n_1$ when $n_1>n_2$. Before using an inverse sine, check the direction of travel and then whether the incident angle measured from the normal exceeds $c$; equality gives a refracted ray along the boundary.

title: Use node voltages for crossed branches
body: Label one node $0\,\mathrm V$ and calculate each other node's potential from known cell rises and resistor drops; the p.d. across a component is then the difference of its end-node values. This is especially useful when a bridge or multiple loops make a memorised potential-divider formula ambiguous; the signed p.d.s around any closed loop must sum to zero.

title: Find a nonlinear operating point by intersection
body: For a lamp or diode with an $I$–$V$ curve in series with a source of emf $E$ and fixed resistance $R$, draw or solve the load line $V=E-IR$. The physical current and component p.d. occur where that line intersects the device curve; check that $0\leq V\leq E$ for a passive device in this simple circuit.

section: 7. A Level: circular motion and gravitation (12–13)
title: Use centre-to-centre radius in orbit calculations
body: For an object at height $h$ above a spherical body's surface, put $r=R+h$ into gravity, orbital speed and period formulae; $h$ alone is not the orbital radius. Check that the calculated $r$ is larger than $R$ and that the near-surface limit gives $r\to R$.

section: 7. A Level: circular motion and gravitation (12–13)
title: Check the sign of gravitational transfer
body: With zero potential at infinity, $U=-GMm/r$ becomes less negative as an object moves outward, so an external agent must supply positive energy $\Delta U=GMm(1/r_1-1/r_2)$ for $r_2>r_1$. This sign check prevents treating the negative potential as a negative energy cost.

section: 8. A Level: gases and thermal physics (14–15)
title: Check a $p$–$V$ cycle by its direction
body: Over a closed cycle, $\Delta U=0$; clockwise traversal gives positive net work done by the gas equal to the enclosed area, and anticlockwise traversal gives negative net work by the gas. Heat added minus heat rejected must have the same sign and magnitude as that net work.

title: Make a quarter-cycle state table
body: For SHM starting at $x=+A$, mark states at $t=0,T/4,T/2,3T/4$: displacement $+A,0,-A,0$ and velocity $0,-v_{\max},0,+v_{\max}$. The signs expose a wrong phase or acceleration direction without differentiating the whole expression.

section: 10. A Level: electric fields and capacitance (17–18)
title: Ask whether the capacitor stays connected
body: When plate spacing or dielectric changes, a capacitor connected to an ideal battery keeps $V$ fixed, whereas an isolated charged capacitor keeps $Q$ fixed. Use $U=\tfrac12CV^2$ in the first case and $U=Q^2/(2C)$ in the second; checking which quantity is constrained prevents a reversed energy prediction.

section: 10. A Level: electric fields and capacitance (17–18)
title: Separate electric field from potential at symmetry points
body: At the midpoint between two equal like point charges, their field vectors cancel but their scalar potentials add; between equal unlike charges, the potentials cancel while the fields reinforce. Sketch arrows for $\mathbf E$ and add signed numbers for $V$ before calculating either.

title: Magnetic force changes direction, not speed
body: For a charge moving in a magnetic field alone, $\mathbf F=q\mathbf v\times\mathbf B$ is perpendicular to the instantaneous velocity, so its work and change in kinetic energy are zero. A computed increase in speed requires an electric field or another force; only the path direction can change under the magnetic force.

title: Integrate an induced-emf pulse
body: For a fixed coil with flux linkage changing between two states, the signed area under an emf–time graph equals $-\Delta(N\Phi)$, even if the pulse height varies. The area of a return pulse must undo the first area if the flux linkage ends at its initial value.

section: 12. A Level: quantum, nuclear, medical, astronomy (22–25)
title: Subtract two photoelectric experiments
body: For the same emitting surface, subtract $eV_s=hf-\Phi$ at two frequencies to eliminate the unknown work function: $e(V_{s,2}-V_{s,1})=h(f_2-f_1)$. Check that higher frequency gives the larger stopping-potential magnitude, provided both frequencies exceed threshold.

section: 12. A Level: quantum, nuclear, medical, astronomy (22–25)
title: Cancel electrons in atomic-mass calculations
body: If a nuclear reaction has the same total proton number on both sides, neutral atomic masses may be used throughout because the total electron masses cancel. If positrons or bare nuclei enter the bookkeeping, first check the particle convention and account for electron masses consistently before taking the small mass difference.

section: 12. A Level: quantum, nuclear, medical, astronomy (22–25)
title: Use thickness differences to remove incident intensity
body: For one material with constant attenuation coefficient, measurements at $x_1$ and $x_2$ satisfy $\mu=\ln(I_1/I_2)/(x_2-x_1)$, so the unknown initial intensity cancels. Check that $I_2<I_1$ when $x_2>x_1$ and the resulting $\mu$ is positive.

section: 12. A Level: quantum, nuclear, medical, astronomy (22–25)
title: Combine brightness and temperature before solving for stellar radius
body: From $F=L/(4\pi d^2)$ and $L=4\pi r^2\sigma T^4$, obtain $r/d=\sqrt{F/(\sigma T^4)}$ directly. This gives the angular-radius scale without calculating luminosity first; check that a hotter star with the same received flux has a smaller $r/d$.
